overview:
Anubhaga-bandha (also spelled anubhāga-bandha) is a technical term in Jain karmic theory that refers to the bondage of karma with respect to its intensity or fruition-power. Within the broader doctrine of bandha (bondage), Jain philosophers distinguish four parameters by which karmic bondage is analyzed: prakṛti (the specific type or species of karma), sthiti (the duration for which karma remains bound), anubhāga (the intensity or fruition-quality of the karmic experience), and pradeśa (the quantity of karmic particles bound to the soul). Anubhaga-bandha thus focuses on how strongly a particular karma will be felt when it matures, rather than how long it lasts or how many particles are involved.

In classical formulations, especially in texts like the Tattvārthasūtra, anubhāga is described as the "fruit-giving power" of karma—the degree to which karmic matter, once bound, is capable of producing a pleasant or painful experience when it ripens. Digambara sources such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and its associated Mahābandha section elaborate this in great detail, explaining that the intensity of karmic fruition is primarily conditioned by the strength of the soul’s passions (kaṣāya) at the time of bondage. Strong anger, pride, deceit, and greed lead to karmas with higher anubhāga, which in turn yield more intense experiences of pleasure or pain when they come into operation.

Anubhaga-bandha is closely tied to the ethical and spiritual state of the jīva (soul). When the soul engages in activities of body, speech, and mind (yoga) under the influence of delusion and passions, it attracts karmic pudgala (subtle matter) and binds it with specific parameters. The nature (prakṛti) and quantity (pradeśa) of karma are largely determined by the kind of activity and its scope, whereas the duration (sthiti) and intensity (anubhāga) are determined by the depth and persistence of passions. Thus, two individuals may commit outwardly similar actions, but if one acts with intense hatred and the other with mild irritation, the resulting karmas will differ significantly in anubhāga, leading to different experiential consequences in future lives.

From the perspective of the soul’s journey through the guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual development), understanding anubhaga-bandha helps explain why some beings experience extremely intense suffering or extraordinary prosperity, while others undergo milder forms of pleasure and pain. High-anubhāga in harmful karmas can manifest as severe physical or mental suffering, low status, or obstructed spiritual progress; high-anubhāga in auspicious karmas can manifest as great beauty, wealth, or influence. Yet, Jain doctrine insists that both auspicious and inauspicious karmas are ultimately forms of bondage that keep the soul in saṃsāra. The spiritual aim is not to seek high-intensity auspicious karmas, but to reduce and ultimately stop all karmic bondage through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.

Technical discussions in Digambara literature, especially in the Anubhāga-bandhādhikāra of the Mahābandha, analyze how different grades of passions and vows correlate with specific ranges of anubhāga for each of the eight main karmas (knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding, obstructive, feeling-producing, body-making, status-determining, and lifespan-determining). These analyses are often highly mathematical and cosmological, describing the infinitesimal pudgala units and their configurations. While such details are accessible only to omniscient beings in their fullness, the texts provide structured rules that allow advanced scholars to reason about karmic intensity in a systematic way.

Modern expositions, drawing on both traditional commentaries and contemporary scholarship, emphasize that anubhaga-bandha should not be confused with mere emotional intensity at the time of experience. It is a property of the karmic bond formed at the time of action, which later conditions the strength of the resultant experience. This distinction helps practitioners understand why cultivating equanimity and reducing passions at the time of action is crucial: even if one cannot yet stop all karmic influx, weakening passions reduces the anubhāga of newly bound karmas, thereby softening future experiences and making spiritual progress more feasible. In this way, anubhaga-bandha serves as a bridge between the subtle metaphysics of karma and the practical ethics of self-restraint and inner transformation in Jainism.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Chapter 8, Bandha)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (sectarian attribution varies)
primary_sources.translation: Bondage (bandha) is characterized by the nature (prakṛti), duration (sthiti), intensity of fruition (anubhāga), and quantity of space-points (pradeśa) of karma.
primary_sources.notes: This sūtra provides the canonical fourfold classification of karmic bondage parameters. The term anubhāga here denotes the intensity or fruition-power of karma, which later Digambara and Śvetāmbara commentators explicitly gloss as the strength of the experience produced when karma matures. Minor textual variants exist (e.g., with or without the final visarga or plural marker), but the semantic content is stable across major editions.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama – Mahābandha, Anubhāga-bandhādhikāra
primary_sources.author: Primary scripture by Ācārya Puṣpadanta and Ācārya Bhūtabali; major commentary Mahādhavala by Ācārya Vīrasena; modern Hindi exposition by Bhūtbali and Fulchandra Jain Śāstrī
primary_sources.original_text: Original Jaina Śaurasenī Prakrit verses are extensive and vary by manuscript; a representative line discussing anubhāga-bandha is transmitted in critical editions but not easily reducible to a single standard citation here.
primary_sources.transliteration: Jaina Śaurasenī Prakrit verses; for example, references to "anubhāga-bandha" occur within the Anubhāga-bandhādhikāra section.
primary_sources.translation: In summary, the Anubhāga-bandhādhikāra explains that anubhāga is the fruit-giving power (phaladāna-śakti) of karma. It teaches that when the soul, under the influence of strong passions (kaṣāya), binds karmic matter, the resulting karmas possess higher intensity of fruition. The text systematically correlates grades of passions and vows with specific ranges of anubhāga for each karmic type, showing how the ethical condition of the soul at the time of bondage determines the strength of future experiences.
primary_sources.notes: The Mahābandha is a Digambara commentary tradition closely linked to the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, considered one of the earliest and most authoritative expositions of karmic doctrine. Modern critical editions note significant manuscript variation, and editors report relying on scarce and sometimes error-prone sources, including copper-plate manuscripts. Because of this, precise wording of individual verses must be checked against specific editions; the summary given here reflects the consensus of contemporary Digambara scholarship rather than a single standardized verse.

primary_sources.title: Doctrine of Karma – First Steps to Jainism (Part-2)
primary_sources.author: Sancheti Asoo Lal Bhandari and Manak Mal (Jainworld educational text)
primary_sources.original_text: The text is originally in modern English prose; no Prakrit or Sanskrit verse is given for anubhāga-bandha in this educational presentation.
primary_sources.translation: “Just as fodder eaten by a cow or goat is converted into milk, which simultaneously determines its taste like sweetness, and other qualities as also its quantity and lastingness or duration, similarly in respect of Karma the nature (Prakriti) duration (Sithi), intensity (Anubhag) and quantity (Pradesh) is determined along with the attachment or Bondage.”
primary_sources.notes: This community-education text, based on traditional doctrine, explains anubhāga in accessible language as the intensity of karmic fruition. It explicitly lists the four aspects of bondage—prakṛti, sthiti, anubhāga, and pradeśa—and uses the analogy of milk’s taste, quantity, and duration to illustrate how karmic bondage simultaneously determines multiple parameters. While not a primary Prakrit/Sanskrit source, it faithfully reflects the classical framework and is widely used in introductory Jain studies.

misconceptions.myth: Anubhaga-bandha is the same as the duration (sthiti) of karma and only tells us how long karma will last.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, anubhāga-bandha is distinct from sthiti-bandha. Sthiti describes how long a karma remains bound to the soul before it matures, whereas anubhāga describes how intense the experience will be when that karma ripens. Two karmas can have the same duration but very different anubhāga, leading to experiences of very different strength.

misconceptions.myth: Anubhaga-bandha is purely quantitative and depends only on how much karmic matter (pradeśa) is bound.
misconceptions.reality: Quantity of karmic particles is analyzed under pradeśa-bandha, not anubhāga-bandha. Anubhāga refers to the qualitative intensity of fruition, which is primarily determined by the strength of passions (kaṣāya) at the time of bondage. A small quantity of karma bound with intense hatred can have higher anubhāga than a larger quantity bound with mild emotion.

misconceptions.myth: Only inauspicious (pāpa) karmas can have high anubhāga; auspicious (puṇya) karmas are always mild in their effects.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts explain that both auspicious and inauspicious karmas can possess high or low anubhāga. High-anubhāga auspicious karmas may result in intense worldly pleasures, beauty, or status, while high-anubhāga inauspicious karmas may result in severe suffering. From the standpoint of liberation, both are forms of bondage; the goal is to reduce and ultimately end all karmic bondage, not to seek high-intensity auspicious experiences.
